prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A man at the center of a mysterious case of exposure to the deadly biological agent ricin has been arrested, FBI spokesman Richard Kolko said Wednesday. Ricin was found in a room in this Las Vegas, Nevada, extended-stay hotel in February, police say. Roger Bergendorff was taken into custody Wednesday morning in Las Vegas, Nevada, Kolko said. Bergendorff, 57, was hospitalized with what was diagnosed as ricin exposure after the agent was discovered in his hotel room off the Las Vegas Strip. Tests conducted by the FBI determined that the substance contained 2.9 percent active ricin. Its preparation was characterized as "crude," according to the U.S. attorney's office in Las Vegas. According to a press release from the Department of Justice office, a search of Bergendorff's hotel room turned up "an 'Anarchist's Cookbook,' a collection of instructions on poisons and other dangerous recipes, including instructions on the preparation of ricin," two semiautomatic pistols, a rifle and a pistol with a silencer. "FBI searches of Salt Lake City [Utah] storage units rented by Von Bergendorff resulted in the discovery of castor beans, various chemicals used in the production of ricin, a respirator, filters, painter's mask, laboratory glassware, syringes and a notebook on ricin production," the Justice Department release said. Bergendorff is charged with possession of a biological toxin, possession of unregistered firearms and possession of firearms not identified by serial number, according to the U.S. attorney's office. If convicted of all charges, he would face a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison and a fine of $750,000. Bergendorff is scheduled for an initial court appearance at 3 p.m. Wednesday. It is illegal under federal law to possess a biological agent and toxin unless it is used for bona fide research or other peaceful purpose, U.S. Attorney Gregory Bower said in a written statement. Bergendorff's cousin, Thomas Tholen of Riverton, Utah, was indicted by a federal grand jury in Salt Lake City this month, accused of failing to report production and possession of ricin. Ricin is a poison that can be made from the waste of castor bean processing, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It can come in the form of a mist or pellet and can be dissolved in water or weak acid, the agency said. Bergendorff was hospitalized February 14 in Las Vegas after he complained of difficulty breathing. He slipped into a coma and awoke March 14. Bergendorff, 57, is an artist who neighbors said had lived in his cousin's basement before moving to Las Vegas. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kevin Bohn, Karan Olson and Carol Cratty contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The man linked to a puzzling ricin exposure investigation has been arrested, FBI spokesman Richard Kolko said Wednesday.

Authorities said ricin was discovered in February inside a room at an extended-stay hotel in Las Vegas, Nevada. Kolko said Roger Bergendorff, 57, was arrested Wednesday morning in Las Vegas.

Bergendorff had been treated at a hospital for what doctors determined was exposure to ricin after the substance was found in his hotel room near the Las Vegas Strip. FBI testing showed the material contained 2.9 percent active ricin. The U.S. attorney’s office in Las Vegas described the substance’s preparation as “crude.”

According to a Justice Department news release, investigators searching Bergendorff’s hotel room found “an ‘Anarchist’s Cookbook,’ a collection of instructions on poisons and other dangerous recipes, including instructions on the preparation of ricin,” along with two semiautomatic handguns, a rifle, and a pistol fitted with a silencer.

The Justice Department also said FBI searches of storage units rented by Von Bergendorff in Salt Lake City, Utah, led agents to castor beans, several chemicals used to make ricin, a respirator, filters, a painter’s mask, laboratory glassware, syringes, and a notebook about producing ricin.

The U.S. attorney’s office said Bergendorff faces charges of possessing a biological toxin, possessing unregistered firearms, and possessing firearms without serial numbers. If found guilty on every count, he could receive up to 30 years in prison and a $750,000 fine.

His first court appearance was set for 3 p.m. Wednesday.

In a written statement, U.S. Attorney Gregory Bower said federal law bars possession of biological agents and toxins unless they are being used for legitimate research or another peaceful purpose.

Bergendorff’s cousin, Thomas Tholen of Riverton, Utah, was indicted earlier this month by a federal grand jury in Salt Lake City. He is accused of not reporting the production and possession of ricin.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says ricin is a poison that can be produced from the waste left over after castor beans are processed. The CDC says it may appear as a mist or pellet and can also be dissolved in water or a weak acid.

Bergendorff was admitted to a Las Vegas hospital on February 14 after saying he was having trouble breathing. He later fell into a coma and regained consciousness on March 14.

Bergendorff, 57, is an artist, and neighbors said he had previously lived in his cousin’s basement before relocating to Las Vegas.

CNN’s Kevin Bohn, Karan Olson, and Carol Cratty contributed to this report.

**Federal Ricin Case in Las Vegas Centered on Hospitalized Motel Resident Roger Von Bergendorff**

**LAS VEGAS —** A 2008 ricin scare that began with a medical emergency at a Las Vegas motel led federal investigators to a small cache of the deadly toxin, castor beans, weapons, and documents describing how ricin is made, according to authorities and court filings in the case of **Roger Von Bergendorff**.

Von Bergendorff, then in his 50s, became the focus of a major federal investigation after he was hospitalized in February 2008 and ricin was later discovered among his belongings at an extended-stay motel.

## Hospitalization and discovery

The case began when Von Bergendorff was taken to a Las Vegas hospital in mid-February 2008 after suffering severe respiratory distress and other symptoms. He was reported to have been critically ill and spent time in intensive care, including a period in which he was unable to speak with investigators.

At the time, he had been living at an **Extended Stay America** motel in Las Vegas. The alarm was raised after a relative retrieved some of Von Bergendorff’s belongings from the motel room and discovered suspicious containers. Authorities were contacted, and hazardous-materials teams, local police, the FBI, and public-health officials responded.

Testing confirmed that material found in the room contained **ricin**, a highly toxic substance derived from castor beans. Ricin can be lethal if inhaled, injected, or ingested in sufficient quantity, and it has no widely available antidote.

The discovery prompted the evacuation and temporary closure of parts of the motel while investigators and hazardous-materials crews secured and decontaminated the scene. Officials said there was no evidence that other motel guests or the general public had been intentionally exposed.

## Evidence found by investigators

According to federal authorities, searches tied to Von Bergendorff uncovered items consistent with ricin production or possession, including:

- **Vials or containers of ricin-containing material**
- **Castor beans**, from which ricin is derived
- Equipment and supplies that investigators said could be used to process castor beans
- Written or printed materials describing ricin and how to produce it
- Firearms and related weapons items, including components that drew additional scrutiny from investigators

Authorities also searched locations connected to Von Bergendorff outside Nevada, including in Utah, where he had previously lived. Investigators said the evidence suggested the ricin had not been newly acquired and may have been in his possession for an extended period.

## Federal charges

Von Bergendorff was charged in federal court in Nevada with **possessing ricin**, a biological toxin, without a lawful purpose. Federal prosecutors alleged he knowingly kept the toxin despite having no legitimate research, medical, defensive, or other lawful reason to possess it.

The case was handled as a federal biological-toxin investigation, though officials repeatedly said they had found **no evidence of a terrorism plot**, no indication that Von Bergendorff intended to attack the public, and no broader conspiracy.

Additional evidence involving weapons and related materials was also reviewed by investigators, but the central charge in the ricin case concerned unlawful possession of the toxin.

## Outcome

Von Bergendorff ultimately faced prosecution for the ricin possession. The case drew national attention because ricin is one of the most dangerous naturally derived toxins and because the substance was found in a public lodging facility after the suspect himself became seriously ill.

Federal officials characterized the incident as serious but contained, emphasizing that the ricin was secured and that there was no confirmed mass exposure.
